summary: Explains how the CLUE protocol and its data channel are used together with existing signaling such as SIP and SDP to set up a telepresence call. It is an experimental document that ties the pieces of CLUE into a working call flow.

plainLanguage.summary: Making a telepresence call has several steps handled by different tools. This document is the instruction sheet showing how to run them together in the right order so the call connects.

questions: how is a clue telepresence call set up
how does clue work with sip and sdp

what is the sdp clue group
subtitle: How a CLUE telepresence call is wired into SIP and SDP, so many camera and screen streams can be controlled together.

tldr.problem: A telepresence room sends and receives several video and audio streams. The CLUE protocol describes and chooses those streams, but SIP and SDP set up the actual media, so the two have to be tied together.
tldr.mechanism: A new SDP group called CLUE ties a data channel and the CLUE-controlled media lines together. Sendonly lines are the sender's Encodings, labelled so CLUE messages can refer to them, and media only flows once SDP and CLUE both agree.
tldr.outcome: The result is a working call flow that falls back cleanly for devices without CLUE. The document is Experimental and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 8848 is an Experimental RFC from January 2021 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It works with the CLUE framework (RFC 8845) and protocol (RFC 8847).

sections.title: What This Document Ties Together
sections.content:
RFC 8848 explains how the CLUE protocol and the CLUE data channel are used together, and with existing signaling such as SIP and the Session Description Protocol (SDP), to produce a telepresence call. CLUE itself is defined elsewhere: the framework is RFC 8845 and the protocol is RFC 8847.

A device signals CLUE support with the sip.clue media feature tag. A CLUE-capable device SHOULD include it in REGISTER requests and OPTION responses, and in INVITE and UPDATE requests and responses. Seeing the tag in a contact field tells you the far end supports CLUE.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of two jobs: one person opens the doors, another says who walks through which door. This document says how they coordinate.

sections.title: The CLUE Group and Controlled Media
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new SDP Grouping Framework extension called CLUE. It is a session-level group attribute. Every media m= line whose mid is in the group is CLUE controlled by the CLUE data channel that is also in the group. Only a single CLUE group is specified.

The data channel is a bidirectional channel carried over SCTP over DTLS. A device wanting CLUE MUST put the mid of one, and only one, data channel m= line in its CLUE group. The data channel in the group, together with the sip.clue tag, also signals that the device wants to upgrade the call to CLUE-controlled media.

Lines outside the group follow the normal SDP offer/answer rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The CLUE group is a guest list. Anything on the list is run by the CLUE control channel; anything off the list works the usual way.

sections.title: Encodings Defined in SDP
sections.content:
A sender signals each Encoding (its ability to encode a stream) with an m= line marked a=sendonly, or a=inactive. Each such line MUST be in the CLUE group and MUST carry a label attribute. Labels must differ from the labels on all other lines in the group, except that a dependent stream such as a Forward Error Correction stream uses the same label as the line it depends on.

The label is the reference used in CLUE messages: advertisement messages list Encodings by it, and configure messages pick an Encoding for a Capture by it. A receiver that wants a stream adds a matching a=recvonly line, which is also in the group but does not need a label.

Until the Media Provider has received a valid CLUE configure message for the stream, it is treated as a=inactive. RTP packets MUST NOT be sent, while STUN, RTCP and DTLS packets still are.
sections.plainLanguage: Each sending slot gets a name tag. The control channel says, use the slot named Left Camera for this picture, and nothing is sent until that order arrives.

sections.title: Offer and Answer Procedures
sections.content:
To start CLUE, the first SDP offer includes a data channel m= line and a CLUE group containing its mid. For interoperability with non-CLUE devices, the initial offer SHOULD NOT include other CLUE-controlled lines and SHOULD include at least one non-CLUE-controlled media line. That advice is waived if the sender has evidence the receiver is CLUE capable.

If both the offer and the answer include the data channel with its mid in a CLUE group, the call is CLUE enabled. Otherwise it is not, and a CLUE-capable device MUST either revert to non-CLUE behaviour or end the call. The answerer decides whether initial non-CLUE media flows by accepting or rejecting those lines.

Later offers can add or activate CLUE-controlled lines, and once CLUE media is negotiated devices SHOULD deactivate matching non-CLUE media by setting its port to 0. CLUE can also be enabled or disabled mid-call. If the CLUE channel fails unexpectedly, implementations SHOULD keep sending and receiving media based on the last negotiated CLUE messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides have to say yes to the guest list. If either says no, they just have a normal call, or hang up.

sections.title: Keeping SDP and CLUE in Step
sections.content:
SDP and CLUE run as independent state machines, so that lost or rewritten messages cannot leave interlocking state machines stuck. A device may therefore see a CLUE message naming an Encoding that is not yet in SDP. It MUST NOT reject a CLUE message only because an encID matches no label. It also MUST NOT delay an SDP exchange waiting for CLUE.

Media is the one place the two must agree. An implementation MUST NOT send a CLUE Capture Encoding unless its most recent SDP exchange has an active media line for it and it has received a CLUE configure message specifying a valid Capture.

Because a new SDP negotiation is costlier than a CLUE message, implementations changing both SHOULD send the CLUE update first.

Mismatches are usually brief, but a device MUST cope if they last indefinitely.
sections.plainLanguage: The two instruction sheets can arrive in any order. You may only start sending when both sheets say go.

sections.title: Security and Extra Details
sections.content:
The main added risk is that an attacker could subvert a CLUE-capable device to send large volumes of media at a victim. CLUE can configure multiple streams, which multiplies the traffic. All CLUE-capable devices MUST support key negotiation and receiver intent assurance via DTLS/SRTP on CLUE-controlled RTP lines, and MUST use it or another mechanism giving receiver intent assurance. Legacy non-CLUE media MAY go unsecured for compatibility with older SIP clients.

The sip.clue tag can help fingerprint a device, so SIP signaling for CLUE sessions SHOULD be encrypted with TLS.

Two further topics are covered. A Media Provider sending switched media for an MCC with defined sources MUST send the originating CaptureID in RTP and RTCP, and a receiver must not be disrupted if it arrives out of step with an advertisement. BUNDLE multiplexing of media onto one 5-tuple is optional and imposes no additional restrictions.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is that nobody can aim a firehose of video at a stranger, so receivers must show they really want the stream.
